subject: Prospective PhD applicant (Fall 2027): what people think can be inferred from what they share
body:
Dear Prof. Li,

I'm finishing an M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University and am applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027. I'm writing because PEACH Lab's work is very close to the question I want to spend a PhD on: what people think can be figured out from what they share, with apps and now with AI chatbots, and whether they would ever get to see it.

I came to this question from the building side. As a research assistant working on a bus ridership forecast, I tried a feature that combined a rider's boarding stop with where their phone tended to be at night, using anonymized location data from apps with one-time opt-in consent. It didn't help the model, so I dropped it. But it pinned many riders to a few blocks, and I doubted anyone who tapped "allow" pictured that. My first step toward studying this from the people side was a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool in a Human-Centered Data Science course. I'm now looking for the training to do it properly.

Several of your lab's projects speak directly to this. The lifecycle-wide position paper's point about inference-time risks and deep inference reaching beyond memorization matches what I saw with the location data. CIDER's focus on people's own disclosure boundaries is close to the question of what people expect to stay private. I'd be especially interested in the human side: how people understand what can be inferred from their conversations with AI, and how systems might show them.

Are you planning to take new PhD students for Fall 2027? If so, I'd be grateful for a short conversation. I'd be happy to send my CV if helpful.

Best regards,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
morgan.reyes@example.edu
